data.checks#What every write checks: Parsing is by program headers (PT_INTERP, PT_DYNAMIC, PT_LOAD), for 32-bit and 64-bit files in both byte orders, so it works on stripped files with no section headers. Every offset and size is checked against the file length without overflowing uint64, and the file is capped at 2 GiB so it is safe on 32-bit hosts. Shared strings are never overwritten. Linkers merge string tails in .dynstr. Zero-padding a slot that another name points into would corrupt that name, so such an edit does not go in place: it grows (below), or, where the file cannot grow, is refused (ErrAmbiguous). Writes are atomic. A temporary file in the same directory is created from the original, only the edited byte ranges are written into it, the mode (including setuid) is applied, and it is renamed over the target. A symlink is followed, so the link survives. --output writes elsewhere instead. The result is verified before the rename. The temporary file is re-parsed and compared with the input: same length, byte-identical outside the ranges the edit declared, the declared ranges holding exactly the intended bytes, and every field the edit did not target reading back unchanged. Otherwise the edit fails with ErrVerify and nothing is renamed. The parser is fuzzed. FuzzParse feeds arbitrary bytes to the parser and to every edit and the verifier; the corpus is committed, and CI replays it and fuzzes for 60 seconds per run.
data.differential#Tested against patchelf:
differential_test.go and differential_growth_test.go build real ELF files with gcc (executables, PIE and not, and shared libraries), apply the same edit with patchelf and with elfpatch, and compare what readelf -d -l -V reports (NEEDED, SONAME, RPATH, RUNPATH, the interpreter, the version-needed file names, the kinds of program header), every --print-* output byte for byte, and that readelf has no complaint about the result. Then the edited program is run with no LD_LIBRARY_PATH; for a library, a program is linked against the edited library and run. In-place edits must not grow the file; growth cases cover long interpreters and rpaths, an rpath where there is none, --add-needed, --set-soname, --replace-needed with version needs, --page-size and combinations.
It runs in CI on Ubuntu against the patchelf from apt, where it is required, and a second job runs the growth cases against patchelf 0.19.3 built from its tag, requiring the same PT_LOAD flags, the same file size and the same program and section header tables as that release. On a machine without Linux, gcc, readelf or patchelf it skips and says why. Nothing binary is committed: the fixtures are built from small C files at test time, and the synthetic images (internal/elfgen, every class and byte order, both layouts) cover what gcc cannot build here.
FuzzGrow feeds arbitrary bytes to the layout engine, the growth edits and the verifier; its corpus is committed and CI fuzzes it for 60 seconds per run.
data.elfpatch#elfpatch:
github.com/go-binfmt/elfpatch is a pure-Go replacement for the subset of NixOS patchelf that package builders use: read and edit the interpreter, RPATH/RUNPATH, DT_SONAME and DT_NEEDED of ELF files, growing the file when a value does not fit. It is a library and a command.
go install github.com/go-binfmt/elfpatch/cmd/elfpatch@latest elfpatch --print-rpath bin/tool elfpatch --set-rpath '$ORIGIN/../lib' bin/tool elfpatch --set-interpreter /lib/ld-musl-x86_64.so.1 bin/tool elfpatch --remove-needed libm.so.6 --shrink-rpath bin/tool elfpatch --add-needed libextra.so.1 --add-rpath '$ORIGIN/../lib' bin/tool elfpatch --set-soname libfoo.so.2 lib/libfoo.so.1 elfpatch --dry-run --set-rpath '$ORIGIN/lib' bin/tool # prints the change, writes nothing The library is github.com/go-binfmt/elfpatch: Open, Parse, Patch, and the File methods Interpreter, Needed, Soname, Rpath, Runpath, SetInterpreter, SetRpath, AddRpath, RemoveRpath, RemoveNeeded, ReplaceNeeded, AddNeeded, SetSoname and ShrinkRpath.
data.grown-verify#What “verified” means for a: The byte-range check of phase 1 cannot judge a file whose layout changed, so the temporary file is judged by structure before the rename: it re-parses; the ELF header is unchanged but for the table offsets and counts; every section keeps its type, flags, links and contents (only .interp, .dynstr and .dynamic may change size, .dynstr only by appending); a section whose address changed must be one patchelf may move; symbols and version names read as before; every untouched field of the snapshot reads back unchanged; and the program headers describe the new file (each allocated section in a PT_LOAD at the offset its address implies, with the permissions its flags need; PT_INTERP, PT_DYNAMIC and PT_PHDR matching; no overlapping or writable-and-executable segment added). Anything else is ErrVerify.
data.performance#Performance:
Measured single core, against patchelf, on the same files. On a 16 KiB file elfpatch is slower, because a Go process starts slower than a C one; on large files it is faster for prints and close to patchelf for edits. The numbers, the machine and the method are in the README, and the small-file gap is tracked in go-binfmt/elfpatch#2.
Growth (CI runner, single core, patchelf 0.18.0, medians of 60 interleaved rounds): patchelf / elfpatch is 0.6x on 16 KiB files, 0.6-0.9x on 4 MiB files (an open defect, go-binfmt/elfpatch#7) and 1.2x on 32 MiB files, for --set-rpath, --add-needed and --set-interpreter.
Licensed BSD-3-Clause.
data.phase-1#In place, verified (phase 1):
A value that fits is written in place: into the slot the linker reserved, zero-padded. A value that does not fit makes the file grow (phase 2, below); a file that cannot be grown refuses with ErrNoSpace (exit 1) and nothing is written. A value is never truncated.
patchelf flag elfpatch --print-interpreter, --print-rpath, --print-needed, --print-soname same output (--print-soname prints nothing, exit 0, when there is none or the file is not a shared object, as patchelf does) --remove-rpath removes the entry (later dynamic entries shift down, as patchelf does) --shrink-rpath drops directories that provide no DT_NEEDED library, and duplicates --remove-needed removes the entries; no match is not an error --version, --output FILE, --dry-run yes (--dry-run is ours) With several operations on one command line, elfpatch applies them in patchelf’s order: soname, interpreter, one rpath operation (shrink, else remove, else set, else add), remove-needed, replace-needed, add-needed.
data.phase-2#Phase 2: growth, the way patchel:
Since v0.3.0 a value that does not fit grows the file. The layout engine is a port of the section-replacement half of patchelf 0.19.3 (replaceSection, rewriteSectionsLibrary, rewriteSectionsExecutable, shiftFile, trimLoadSegments, normalizeNoteSegments, rewriteHeaders):
The new string is appended to .dynstr (or .interp is rewritten, or an entry is added at the top of .dynamic), and the section that grew is replaced by a larger copy placed in new space. A shared library gets that space at the end of the file, in a new PT_LOAD after the last page, or by extending the last PT_LOAD when it is read-write and ends where the file does. An executable cannot move its code, so the sections in front of it (.interp, notes, hash tables, .dynsym, .dynstr) move into the header page, the rest of the file shifts by whole pages, and the header PT_LOAD is reused or split into its own read-write one. The page size comes from e_machine (64 KiB for aarch64, ppc, mips, ia64, alpha, tilegx and loongarch; 8 KiB for sparc; 4 KiB otherwise) or from --page-size. The program and section headers are rewritten and sorted, the addresses in .dynamic follow their sections, and st_shndx follows the new section order. ELF32 and ELF64, both byte orders, executables and shared libraries. Growth needs section headers, as patchelf does.
patchelf flag elfpatch --set-interpreter in place when it fits (patchelf always relocates), else .interp moves --set-rpath (--force-rpath) in place when it fits and nothing else shares the string, else appended to .dynstr; no entry yet: a DT_RUNPATH (DT_RPATH) is added --add-rpath DIRS old:DIRS set as above; adds a DT_RUNPATH when there is none --set-soname shared objects only (patchelf ignores it on ET_EXEC); adds DT_SONAME when there is none --add-needed LIB repeatable; sorted, added at the top of .dynamic, so they are searched first --replace-needed OLD NEW in place when it fits and is unshared, else appended; the version-needed file names follow --page-size N page size for the layout Not done, and refused with nothing written: --set-os-abi, --add-debug-tag, --no-default-lib, --clear-symbol-version, --rename-dynamic-symbols, --build-resolution-cache, a file with a .note.nixos.ldcache note, --set-rpath on a file with both DT_RPATH and DT_RUNPATH, and .gnu.version_r names that live outside .dynstr.
data.sections#Reading section headers: Since v0.5.0, File.Sections() returns the section headers (name, type, flags, address, file offset, size) in file order, read with the decoder the growing edits use; a section that lies outside the image is refused with ErrCorrupt, and an image without a section table (a stripped binary) with ErrUnsupported. fwimg uses it for -j / -R.

data.assurance#Assurance: The writer is tested differentially against dtc and the reader against fdtget, in CI with the tools required so that a runner that loses them fails instead of skipping. Parse is fuzzed with the dtc test suite as the committed corpus, statement coverage is gated at 100 %, and every refusal is mutation swept. Performance is measured in CI against libfdt; the table is in the repository README.
data.fdt#fdt:
github.com/go-binfmt/fdt is a pure-Go reader and writer for devicetree blobs (DTB, format version 17): the format of dtc -O dtb and of the FIT images U-Boot loads. No cgo, no libfdt, no dtc on the build host. It is a library and a command.
go install github.com/go-binfmt/fdt/cmd/fdt@latest fdt check board.dtb # parse, refuse if malformed fdt dump board.dtb # devicetree source on stdout fdt ls board.dtb /cpus # subnodes fdt get board.dtb /cpus/cpu@0 reg # a property (-t s|u32|u64|x picks the format) import "github.com/go-binfmt/fdt" t, err := fdt.Parse(blob) // every bound checked; errors wrap fdt.ErrFormat cpu, _ := t.Find("/cpus/cpu@0") reg, _ := cpu.Uint32s("reg") cpu.SetString("status", "okay") out, _ := t.Marshal() // byte-identical to dtc for the same tree
data.reading#Reading: Parse takes untrusted bytes. Every header field, the reservation map, the structure block and the strings block are checked against the input length without overflowing, so the result is the same on 32-bit hosts. Nesting deeper than MaxDepth (128), duplicate node or property names, misaligned or overlapping blocks, a truncated or unknown token and a second root are refused. Versions 17 and 16 are read; anything older is ErrVersion. Nothing is truncated or guessed.
data.writing#Writing: Marshal writes the layout dtc writes, including its string table, so the result is byte-identical to dtc -I dts -O dtb for the same tree. CI proves it against the real dtc on random trees and on the blobs of dtc’s own test suite. For large payloads, ParseShared and AppendMarshal avoid the copies that Parse and Marshal make.

data.benchmark#Benchmark:
Against objcopy (reference / fwimg, so more than 1x means fwimg is faster; linux/arm64, one core, medians of 40 rounds):
File binary srec ihex uimage 1 KiB 0.7x 0.7x 0.7x 2.9x 4 MiB 1.1x 1.2x 1.2x 8.8x 32 MiB 1.0x 1.2x 1.1x 13.3x Reading text (-I ihex / -I srec to a flat binary) on the CI runner (Ubuntu x86-64, objcopy 2.46, 60 rounds, one core; the bench job of run 45888191102 on go-binfmt/fwimg main at 2d5d60c2d0f0, v0.4.3):
File -O binary -I ihex -I srec 1 KiB 0.6x 0.6x 0.6x 4 MiB 0.9x 1.6x 1.5x 32 MiB 1.0x 1.7x 1.5x On the same runner the -O srec and -O ihex rows are 1.1x at 4 MiB and 1.3x at 32 MiB. The flat binary was 0.5x and 0.6x at 4 and 32 MiB before v0.4.2 (go-binfmt/fwimg#17: it built a second image and truncated an existing output in place); v0.4.2 streams the segments and unlinks the output first, v0.4.3 maps an ELF input. The 4 MiB flat row is still behind by about 0.3 ms, a start-up cost of the Go runtime, like the 1 KiB rows, tracked in go-binfmt/fwimg#2. See the README for the method.
data.fwimg#fwimg:
github.com/go-binfmt/fwimg converts an ELF executable into the image a bootloader or ROM loads at a fixed address: a flat binary (objcopy -O binary), a Motorola S-record, Intel HEX or a legacy U-Boot uImage (mkimage, optionally gzip or lz4 compressed), a UF2 file (uf2conv.py) or a Verilog hex memory file (objcopy -O verilog). It is a library and a command, in pure Go, with no binutils, srec_cat or mkimage on the build host.
It moved here from go-coff/peln/fwimg, which is now deprecated; pectl objcopy uses this module.
go install github.com/go-binfmt/fwimg/cmd/fwimg@latest import "github.com/go-binfmt/fwimg" elf, _ := os.ReadFile("kernel.elf") flat, base, err := fwimg.Flatten(bytes.NewReader(elf), int64(len(elf)), fwimg.FlattenOptions{}) Flatten takes the size of the input; SREC, IHEX and UImage return an error.
data.input#Reading other formats:
The input does not have to be an ELF. fwimg recognises an ELF, an Intel HEX file, an S-record file and a uImage by their magic or syntax, so any of them converts to any output; -I forces the format. A raw file is never guessed: it needs -I binary --base ADDR, as objcopy -I binary needs its address.
fwimg -I ihex -O binary -o fw.bin fw.hex fwimg -I binary --base 0x8000000 -O srec -o fw.srec fw.bin fwimg info uImage # the header, as `mkimage -l` prints it In Go, DecodeIHEX, DecodeSREC, ParseUImage, RawImage and Detect return an Image of sparse segments (with the entry point and the name), which EncodeSREC and EncodeIHEX write back.
The decoders check what the formats define and say where it fails: checksums (with the line number), the end record, the S5/S6 count, both uImage CRCs and the size table of a multi-file image, which is bounded by the header’s size. Overlapping records and data past 4 GiB are refused, not merged or wrapped. They are checked against objcopy -I, srec_cat, mkimage -l and dumpimage in CI, and fuzzed.
data.l5#UF2, Verilog hex and compressed uImag:
Since v0.7.0:
fwimg -O uimage --uimage-comp gzip --load 0x80000 --entry 0x80000 -o uImage kernel.elf fwimg -O uimage --uimage-comp lz4 --load 0x80000 --entry 0x80000 -o uImage kernel.elf fwimg -O uf2 --uf2-family rp2040 -o fw.uf2 fw.elf # a family name or a number fwimg -O verilog --verilog-data-width 4 -o mem.hex fw.elf fwimg -I uf2 -O binary -o fw.bin fw.uf2 fwimg -I verilog --verilog-data-width 4 -O ihex -o fw.hex mem.hex --uimage-comp none|gzip|lz4 compresses the payload and sets ih_comp (gzip 1, lz4 5); ih_size and the data CRC cover the compressed bytes, as mkimage does. The gzip stream is reproducible (no time, no name, a fixed level). Reading a compressed uImage decompresses it, bounded by --max-size: a decompression bomb is refused, not expanded, and a payload marked gzip that is not gzip is refused (ErrSyntax). info, verify and --json describe the decompressed program; the listing keeps the header as stored. -O uf2 writes uf2conv.py’s layout: blocks of 256 payload bytes, cut where the next segment starts, each padded with zeros. --uf2-family NAME|NUMBER sets the family ID (the table is the one of microsoft/uf2 at a pinned commit; 0 is refused). The reader is strict: magics, block numbers, the block count and the flags are checked, and a file container or a not-main-flash block is refused. -O verilog is objcopy’s $readmemh layout: @ADDRESS lines in uppercase hex, CRLF line ends. --verilog-data-width 1..8 is the word width in bytes, --verilog-endian little|big orders the bytes within a word. Segment addresses must be multiples of the width. The reader accepts // and /* */ comments, @ addresses and _ digit separators, and refuses a token wider than a word. The readers are fuzzed. CI compares the output with mkimage (the compressed header: mkimage -C only tags ih_comp, it does not compress), uf2conv.py and objcopy -O verilog (little-endian output), and the lane fails if a reference tool is missing. The manifest schema lists uf2 and verilog as formats. In Go: EncodeUF2, DecodeUF2, VerifyUF2, EncodeVerilog, DecodeVerilog, CompressPayload, DecompressPayload, UF2Families and ParseUF2Family.
data.manifest#Manifest, info and verify:
Since v0.6.0 an image can be described, listed and checked later:
fwimg -O ihex --manifest fw.json -o fw.hex fw.elf # the image, described fwimg info fw.hex # any input: format, start, ranges, hashes fwimg info --json fw.elf # the same facts, as a manifest fwimg verify --manifest fw.json fw.hex # re-read an image, check every hash fwimg verify --manifest fw.json -I binary --base 0x8000000 fw.bin The manifest is JSON in a fixed key order: format, base, entry (null without one), pad, size, data_size, the CRC-32 and SHA-256 of the whole image, and for each segment (and each --region) its address, size, source file and both hashes. An ELF input adds its allocated sections, and a uImage output its header fields. The same input and options give the same bytes: there is no timestamp unless SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH is set, and then created is that time in UTC. Addresses are strings ("0x8000000", lowercase hex), because a JSON number cannot hold 64 bits; sizes are integers. The hashes are of the flat image from base, gaps filled with pad, which is what -O binary writes. The schema is manifest-1.schema.json (JSON Schema 2020-12, additionalProperties: false everywhere), also embedded in the library as fwimg.ManifestSchema. A change that is not backward compatible is manifest-2; schema_version says which one a file is. info reads an ELF, Intel HEX, S-record, uImage or (-I binary --base) a raw file. A uImage is listed as mkimage -l does; the others as text or, with --json, as the manifest. Its ranges and start address are compared with srec_info in CI. verify recomputes, from the image in whatever format it is in, the base, size, start address and the hashes of the whole image and of every segment and region, and lists every difference (exit status 1). A manifest written for the S-record checks the flat binary of the same image. data_size is not compared, because a flat binary counts its padding; the start address is compared only if the image has one. The manifest reader is bounded (16 MiB, 65536 entries per list), refuses unknown keys, and is fuzzed. In Go: NewManifest, ReadManifest, (*Manifest).JSON and Verify, ELFManifestSections and UImageStored.
data.options#objcopy’s options:
Since v0.4.0 the options that shape an image are objcopy’s, with the same names, and the S-record and Intel HEX output is byte for byte what objcopy writes (the S0 header text aside), CRLF included with --crlf:
fwimg -O srec -j '.text*' -j .rodata -o fw.srec fw.elf # keep sections; * and ? match fwimg -O srec -R '.*' -R '!.text' -o fw.srec fw.elf # drop sections; ! protects fwimg -O srec --gap-fill 0xff --pad-to 0x90400 -o fw.srec fw.elf fwimg -O ihex --change-addresses 0x100 -o fw.hex fw.elf # --adjust-vma: the same fwimg -O ihex --set-start 0x80010 -o fw.hex fw.elf # --change-start N: an increment fwimg -O srec --srec-addr-len auto --srec-count --crlf -o fw.srec fw.elf fwimg -O ihex --ihex-mode objcopy --crlf -o fw.hex fw.elf -j and -R select by section name and need an ELF with section headers (read with elfpatch v0.5.0); giving both is refused, as objcopy calls it undefined. --srec-addr-len 16|24|32|auto picks S1/S9, S2/S8 or S3/S7 (auto: the shortest that holds the highest address, as objcopy does); --srec-count adds the S5 (or S6) count record, as srec_cat does. --ihex-mode linear (the default) writes type 04 and type 05 records, as srec_cat; objcopy writes type 02 below 1 MiB and a type 03 start record. An ELF’s entry address is now written to Intel HEX; before v0.4.0 it was dropped. Line endings stay LF unless --crlf is given. In Go: ELFImage, ELFSections with a SectionSelect, EncodeSRECOpts and EncodeIHEXOpts, and Image.GapFill, PadTo and Offset. The options are compared with objcopy 2.44 and srec_cat 1.64 in CI (the lane fails if a tool is missing).
data.playground#Try it in your browser: The fwimg playground runs the real command, built for WebAssembly (GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm, v0.8.0), in a Web Worker: pick an ELF, Intel HEX, S-record, uImage, UF2 or Verilog file, choose a format and the options, and download the result. Nothing is uploaded: the page makes no request that carries your file, its Content-Security-Policy allows no other origin, and the input is limited to 32 MiB. The playground produces the same bytes as the native build (a test compares exit code, output and messages on every release); the release also carries a wasip1 build for wazero and wasmtime.
data.refusals#What it refuses:
The input is untrusted, so the module refuses rather than guesses:
an image whose size comes from attacker-controlled addresses is bounded before it is allocated (FlattenOptions.MaxSize, a caller-stated limit); a segment that lies outside the input; an address range that wraps; SREC and Intel HEX data that would pass 4 GiB, instead of wrapping; text records that arrive scattered, each separate piece being charged against the same size limit.
data.safety#Safety checks:
Since v0.5.0:
A gap refusal names the PT_LOAD segments and sections with LMA and VMA and says which of --use-vaddr or -R .data fits; --gap-warn N (default 8) warns when a hole is more than N times the payload. --region NAME=START:SIZE (repeatable, K/M suffixes) refuses a segment that overflows its region or lies outside every region, naming the segment and the byte excess, in ld’s wording. The output is read back and compared byte for byte with what was written, after every write; on a mismatch there is an error and no file. For S-record, Intel HEX and uImage the file is decoded only when the bytes differ, to name the first differing address (start address included). --no-verify turns it off. Non-regular outputs (devices, symlinks) are not read back. SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH sets the uImage time as mkimage does; an invalid value is refused. Unset, the time is 0, where mkimage uses the input’s mtime.
